title: The wagon-wheel effect
hook: Wheels on film can seem to spin backwards while the car speeds forwards.
peek: In old westerns the stagecoach wheels often appear to turn slowly backwards. The camera is to blame: it takes separate snapshots, and if each spoke moves almost one full gap between frames, it looks like it slipped back a little.
lede: Film is a series of still pictures, usually 24 a second. A spoked wheel looks identical each time it turns by one spoke's spacing, so the camera cannot tell how far it really went. If a spoke moves just short of the next spoke's old position between frames, the brain picks the shortest path and sees the wheel creeping backwards.

bullets.text: At film's standard rate, a wheel with 12 spokes looks frozen if it turns exactly one spoke's spacing per frame, which is 2 turns a second. A little slower and it seems to creep backwards; a little faster and it creeps forwards.

Engineers call this aliasing: sampling a repeating motion too slowly to capture it faithfully. The same effect can make helicopter blades seem to hang motionless in videos when the frame rate matches the blades' rhythm.

Record turntables put the effect to work. Rings of dots on the platter's edge look still under mains-powered light, which flickers at a steady rate, only when the platter spins at exactly the right speed.
Some people see wheels reverse under steady sunlight, with no camera or flicker involved. Researchers have argued about why since the 1960s, and there is still no agreed explanation.
